page: Vultr vhp-2c-4gb-intel is a High Performance family virtual server featuring 2 vCPUs and 4.0 GB of RAM. It is powered by an Intel Xeon x86_64 processor operating at 2.0 GHz, configured with 1 physical core and 2 threads per core under a shared CPU allocation model. The processor includes 32 KB L1d cache, 4 MB L2 cache, and 16 MB L3 cache, supporting instruction sets such as AVX, AVX512F, AVX512_VNNI, AES, and BMI2. Local storage is bundled with 100 GB of NVMe SSD capacity, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Performance benchmarks position this server in the lower tiers. In stress-ng CPU tests, both single-core and multi-core performance fall into the bottom 25% category. Memory bandwidth tests show a significant performance drop-off between cached and uncached operations, with small-block cached reads reaching 190.16 GB/sec (bottom 25%) while large-block uncached reads and writes drop to 11.67 GB/sec and 9.16 GB/sec respectively, placing them in the bottom 10%. Geekbench testing reflects similar constraints, with multi-core, software compilation, ray tracing, and image processing scores all ranking in the bottom 10%.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the server offers an accessible entry point for workloads requiring local NVMe storage without demanding high-performance compute resources. The inclusion of 100 GB of NVMe SSD storage relative to the 4.0 GB RAM allocation provides a favorable storage-to-memory ratio for budget-conscious deployments. However, the shared CPU allocation and weak multi-threaded performance present a clear tradeoff for compute-intensive tasks.

This server is best suited for lightweight, non-critical workloads. Appropriate use cases include basic static web serving, small-scale Redis caching, simple text processing, and entry-level development or testing environments that do not require sustained high CPU or memory throughput.

Benchmark results place this server's compute and memory performance primarily in the bottom 10% to 25% cohorts, with notable bottlenecks in uncached memory bandwidth and multi-core processing. While it offers a cost-effective option for deployments requiring a generous local storage footprint relative to memory, the shared CPU architecture limits its suitability for intensive workloads. It is best utilized for lightweight applications such as static web serving, basic Redis operations, and development environments.
